newsitem.title: CHINA: HK tourism industry crumpled during handover period.
newsitem.headline: HK tourism industry crumpled during handover period.

text.p: Hong Kong's tourism industry shot itself in the foot in June and July by jacking up prices and creating the impression the city was fully booked for the territory's lavish handover celebrations, tourism officials said on Friday.
As a result, fewer people came, and the industry suffered a punishing blow during the two months when tourism -- Hong Kong's biggest foreign currency earner -- plummeted.
Tourism analysts say the industry only has itself to blame.
Months or years before Britain handed Hong Kong back to China on July 1, travel agents and hotels had boasted so much about the tide of guests that real visitors stayed away, they said.

"Everyone in the tourism industry, everyone assumed it would be booming this summer. I would say the misforecasting caught everyone by surpass," Howard Young, who represents the travel industry's interests in the Hong Kong legislature, told Reuters.
"This time last year, if you asked any overseas or local travel agent, they were screaming, saying you probably can't get a room if you don't book early. You might as well forget it."
For what was meant to be the bash of the century, Hong Kong hoteliers and travel operators took a bashing of a different kind.
In June, room occupancy plunged to 70 percent, way below the 87 percent seen in June a year earlier, and 88 percent for the whole of 1996, Hong Kong Tourist Association (HKTA) figures show.
Visitor arrivals to the territory plunged in June to 789,060, down 14 percent from 919,093 in June 1996.
July figures are not yet available but a hotel industry official said room occupancy was around a paltry 60 percent.
The industry's woes appear to be largely self-inflicted.
Anticipating a gush of walk-in visitors around the handover, most hotels decided to cut down block bookings usually reserved for tour groups, Young said. Many hotels then jacked up room rates.
"It was mainly that they did not offer so many rooms for agents. It is no secret that group prices are much cheaper than individual prices," Young said.
With 93 member hotels in the HKTA comprising 35,101 rooms, the tourism industry was Hong Kong's largest foreign currency earning sector in 1996, raking in HK$104.78 billion (US$13.5 billion).
The territory also has many hotels that are not members of the HKTA.
Britain's historic handover of its colony to China at a midnight extravaganza on the evening of June 30 was billed as Asia's party of the century.
"There was this perception because this was such a major event that Hong Kong would automatically be filled up," said HKTA spokesman Peter Randall.
"That was a major misconception all around the world," Randall said, adding that many hotels were "fully booked" by the end of December -- but only in theory.
"When we got into 1997, as tour operators realised perhaps there wasn't as big a demand as they had anticipated, a lot of those hotel rooms were returned," Randall said.
